source_text: Τὴν γὰρ στερρότητα καὶ ἀντιτυπίαν τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ ἐναπολαμβανομένου ταῖς κοιλότησι τῶν νεφῶν, καὶ διὰ τὸ βιαίως ἐκρήγνυσθαι τοὺς κατὰ τὰς βροντὰς ἀποτελοῦντος ψόφους, στερέωσιν βροντῆς ἡ Γραφὴ προσηγόρευσεν. Καὶ νῦν τοίνυν ἡγούμεθα ἐπί τινος στερρᾶς φύσεως, στέγειν τοῦ ὕδατος τὸ ὀλισθηρὸν καὶ εὐδιάλυτον ἐξαρκούσης, τὴν φωνὴν ταύτην τετάχθαι. Καὶ οὐ δήπου, ἐπειδὴ κατὰ τὴν κοινὴν ἐκδοχὴν ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος δοκεῖ τὴν γένεσιν ἐσχηκέναι, ἢ ὕδατι πεπηγότι ἐμφερὲς εἶναι προσήκει νομίζειν, ἤ τινι τοιαύτῃ ὕλῃ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ὑγροῦ διηθήσεως τὴν ἀρχὴν λαμβανούσῃ, ὁποία ἐστὶν ἥ τε τοῦ κρυστάλλου λίθου, ὃν δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος πῆξιν μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν, ἢ ἡ τοῦ σπέκλου φύσις ἐν μετάλλοις συνισταμένη. Λίθος δέ ἐστι διαυγὴς, ἰδιάζουσαν καὶ καθαρωτάτην τὴν διαφάνειαν κεκτημένος, ὃς ἐὰν κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν ἀκριβὴς εὑρεθῇ, μήτε κατεδηδεσμένος σηπεδόνι τινὶ, μήτε τὸ βάθος ὑπερρηγμένος ταῖς διαφύσεσι, μικροῦ τῷ ἀέρι τὴν διαύγειαν ἔοικεν. Οὐδενὶ οὖν τούτων εἰκάζομεν τὸ στερέωμα. Παιδικῆς γὰρ τῷ ὄντι καὶ ἁπλῆς διανοίας, τοιαύτας ἔχειν περὶ τῶν οὐρανίων τὰς ὑπολήψεις. Οὐ μὴν, οὐδὲ εἰ πάντα ἐν ἅπασίν ἐστι, πῦρ μὲν ἐν γῇ, ἀὴρ δὲ ἐν ὕδατι, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὡσαύτως ἐν ἑτέρῳ τὸ ἕτερον· καὶ μηδὲν τῶν αἰσθήσει ὑποπιπτόντων στοιχείων εἰλικρινές ἐστι καὶ ἀμιγὲς, ἢ τῆς πρὸς τὸ μέσον, ἢ τῆς πρὸς τὸ ἀντι κείμενον κοινωνίας· τούτου ἕνεκεν καταδεχόμεθα, τὸ στερέωμα ἢ ἐξ ἑνὸς τῶν ἁπλῶν, ἢ τὸ ἀπὸ τούτων μίγμα φῆσαι ὑπάρχειν, δεδιδαγμένοι παρὰ τῆς Γραφῆς, μηδὲν ἐπιτρέπειν ἡμῶν τῷ νῷ πέρα τῶν συγκεχωρημένων φαντασιοῦσθαι. Μὴ παραδράμῃ δὲ ἡμᾶς μηδὲ ἐκεῖνο ἀπαρασήμαντον, ὅτι μετὰ τὸ προστάξαι τὸν Θεὸν, Γενηθήτω στερέωμα, οὐκ εἴρηται ἁπλῶς, καὶ ἐγένετο στερέωμα· ἀλλὰ, Καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα· καὶ πάλιν, Διεχώρισεν ὁ Θεός. Οἱ κωφοὶ ἀκούσατε, καὶ οἱ τυφλοὶ ἀναβλέψατε. Καὶ τίς κωφὸς, ἀλλ' ἢ ὁ μὴ ἀκούων οὕτω μεγαλοφώνως ἐμβοῶντος τοῦ Πνεύματος; Καὶ τίς τυφλός; Ὁ μὴ ἐνορῶν ταῖς οὕτως ἐναργέσι περὶ τοῦ Μονογενοῦς ἀποδείξεσι. Γενηθήτω στερέωμα. Αὕτη ἡ φωνὴ τῆς προκαταρκτικῆς αἰτίας. Ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα. Αὕτη τῆς ποιητικῆς καὶ δημιουργικῆς δυνάμεως μαρτυρία. 3.5 Ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τὰ συνεχῆ τῆς ἐξηγήσεως τὸν λόγον ἐπανα γάγωμεν. Ἔστω διαχωρίζον, φησὶν, ἀνὰ μέσον ὕδατος καὶ ὕδατος. Ἄπειρος μὲν ἦν, ὡς ἔοικε, τῶν ὑδάτων ἡ χύσις, πανταχόθεν ἐπικυμαινόντων τῇ γῇ καὶ ἀπαιωρουμένων αὐτῆς· ὡς καὶ τὴν πρὸς τὰ ἄλλα στοιχεῖα δοκεῖν ἀναλογίαν ἐκβαίνειν. Διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν ἐλέγετο ἄβυσσος πανταχόθεν περιβεβλῆσθαι τῇ γῇ. Τὴν δὲ αἰτίαν τοῦ πλήθους ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς ἀποδώσομεν. Πάντως δὲ οὐδεὶς ὑμῶν οὐδὲ τῶν πάνυ κατησκημένων τὸν νοῦν, καὶ περὶ τὴν φθειρομένην ταύτην καὶ ῥέουσαν φύσιν ὀξυωπούντων, ἐπισκήψει τῇ δόξῃ, ὡς ἀδύνατα ἢ πλασματώδη ὑποτιθεμένων κατὰ τὸν λόγον· οὐδὲ ἀπαιτήσει ἡμᾶς εὐθύνας, ἐπὶ τίνος ἡ τῶν ὑδάτων ἥδραστο φύσις. Ὧ γὰρ λόγῳ τὴν γῆν βαρυτέραν οὖσαν τοῦ ὕδατος ἀπαιωροῦσι τοῦ μέσου τῶν ἐσχάτων ἀπάγοντες, τῷ αὐτῷ δήπου πάντως καὶ τὸ μυρίον ὕδωρ ἐκεῖνο, διά τε τὴν κατὰ φύσιν ἐπὶ τὸ κάτω φορὰν, καὶ διὰ τὴν πανταχόθεν ἰσορροπίαν, περὶ τὴν γῆν ἀτρεμεῖν συγχωρήσουσιν.
thought_title: The firmament is solid but not ice or crystal
orientation: Basil is explaining the firmament God commands on the second day to divide water from water.
pass_a_gloss: For the solidity and resistance of the wind enclosed in the hollows of the clouds, and through bursting out violently producing the noises at thunders, Scripture named 'making-firm of thunder'. And now therefore we consider this word to have been set upon some solid nature sufficient to cover (contain) the slipperiness and easy dissolution of water. And surely not, since according to the common acceptance it seems to have had its genesis from water, is it fitting to think it either like congealed water or like some such matter taking its beginning from the straining of the moist, such as is that of crystal stone, which they say is transformed through excessive freezing of water, or the nature of mica forming in mines. It is a transparent stone, possessing a peculiar and most pure translucence, which if found exact according to its own nature, neither eaten through by some rot nor broken through in depth by fissures, is nearly like the air in clearness. To none of these then do we liken the firmament. For it is of a childish and simple mind truly to have such suppositions about the heavenly things. Not indeed, not even if all things are in all, fire in earth, air in water, and of the others likewise the one in the other, and none of the elements falling under sense is pure and unmixed of the sharing either toward the middle or toward the opposite, for this reason do we accept to say that the firmament exists either from one of the simple ones or the mixture from them, having been taught by Scripture to permit our mind to imagine nothing beyond the things conceded. Let not that either run past us unmarked, that after God commanded, Let a firmament come to be, it was not said simply, and a firmament came to be, but, And God made the firmament; and again, God separated. The deaf, hear, and the blind, look up. And who is deaf except the one not hearing the Spirit crying out so loudly? And who blind? The one not looking into the so evident demonstrations concerning the Only-begotten. Let a firmament come to be: this the voice of the pre-originating cause. God made the firmament: this testimony of the making and craftsman power. But let us lead back the discourse to the continuation of the exegesis. Let it be separating, he says, between water and water. Boundless was, as it seems, the pouring of the waters, from all sides billowing over the earth and hanging above it, so as to seem to exceed the proportion toward the other elements. For this was said in the foregoing, the abyss was thrown around the earth on all sides. The cause of the quantity we shall give in what follows. Surely none of you, not even of those very exercised in mind and sharp-sighted about this perishing and flowing nature, will censure the opinion as of people supposing impossible or fictitious things in the account; nor will he demand accounts of us, upon what the nature of the waters was seated. For by what reason they suspend the earth, being heavier than water, in the middle, leading it away from the extremes, by the same surely they will also grant that that immense water, through the natural motion downward and through the equal balance from all sides, is at rest around the earth.

choices.why: στερέωσις is the act of making firm, parallel to making firm the wind caught in clouds, not the created firmament

choices.english: we hold that this utterance has been appointed
choices.why: ἡγούμεθα is an opinion verb and τετάχθαι is perfect passive infinitive of appointment, keeping who judges and what was done
rejected: we are led to a solid nature

choices.why: προκαταρκτική distinguishes the commanding voice Let there be from the executive making, as first cause versus effecting power
both adjectives describe productive divine efficacy attested by God made, not human artistry

choices.english: drawing it away from the outermost bounds
choices.why: ἀπάγοντες is active participle of leading away, so the earth is held in the middle by being drawn away from extremes

pass_b_english: For the solidity and resistance of the wind that is caught in the hollows of the clouds, and that makes the crashes of thunder because it bursts out violently, Scripture called the “making firm of thunder” (Amos 4:13). So here too we hold that this word has been set for a solid nature, strong enough to hold in what is slippery and easily dispersed in water.

And surely, because in the common understanding it seems to have had its origin from water, we ought not to think that it is like frozen water, or like some such matter that takes its beginning from the filtering of moisture: such as crystal stone, which they say is transformed by an extreme freezing of water, or the nature of the mica that forms in mines. This is a transparent stone with a clearness of its own, very pure; if it is found perfect according to its nature, neither eaten away by any decay nor split in its depth by cracks, its clearness is almost like the air. We liken the firmament to none of these. For it truly belongs to a childish and simple mind to hold such notions about the heavenly things. Nor, even if all things are in all things, fire in earth and air in water, and likewise each of the others in another, and none of the elements that fall under the senses is pure and unmixed with a share either of the middle element or of its opposite, do we on that account accept the claim that the firmament is made either of one of the simple elements or of a mixture of them. For we have been taught by Scripture to allow our mind to imagine nothing beyond what has been granted.

Let us not pass over this either without marking it: after God commanded, “Let there be a firmament,” it is not said simply, “and there was a firmament,” but, “And God made the firmament” (Genesis 1:6-7); and again, “God divided” (Genesis 1:7). “You deaf, hear; and you blind, look up” (Isaiah 42:18). And who is deaf, but the one who does not hear the Spirit crying out so loudly? And who is blind? The one who does not look into such clear proofs about the Only-begotten. “Let there be a firmament”: this is the voice of the originating cause. “God made the firmament”: this is the testimony of the making and creating power.

But let us bring our discourse back to the course of the explanation. “Let it divide,” he says, “between water and water” (Genesis 1:6). The outpouring of the waters was, it seems, boundless, surging over the earth from every side and hanging above it, so that it seemed to go beyond its proportion to the other elements. That is why it was said earlier that the deep was thrown around the earth on every side. The reason for so great a quantity we shall give in what follows. Surely none of you, not even those whose minds are highly trained and who are keen-sighted about this perishable and flowing nature, will attack the view as if we were proposing impossible or made-up things in our account, or demand that we answer for what the nature of the waters rested on. For by the same reasoning by which they hold the earth, though heavier than water, suspended in the middle, drawing it away from the outer bounds, they will surely grant that that vast water also stays motionless around the earth, both because of its natural motion downward and because of its balance on every side.
notes: spacing splits in source read as single words: ἀντι κείμενον as ἀντικείμενον, ἐπανα γάγωμεν as ἐπαναγάγωμεν; gloss follows normal sense, no text invented

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix-b): third-person insertions ('Basil says we hold...', 'Basil says we liken...', 'Basil says we do not accept...', 'Basil asks who is deaf...', 'Basil says let us return...', 'Basil says he will give the reason...') removed; the Greek is first person throughout. Retranslated clause by clause (alert item 9; amos/SOURCE_ISSUES.md item 1). Amos 4:13 kept: the LXX of that verse reads 'ὁ στερεῶν βροντήν' (the one making firm the thunder); the KJV follows the Hebrew ('he that formeth the mountains').

problems.why: The phrase 'strengthening/establishing thunder' is from Amos 4:13 (LXX). Job 37:4 does not say it.

problems.quote: People say crystal is changed into stone by the extreme freezing of water.
problems.source_quote: ὃν δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος πῆξιν μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν
problems.why: Reverses direction: water freezes into crystal, not crystal into stone.
problems.fix: People say water is turned into crystal stone by extreme freezing.
problems.ruling: ὃν δι' ὑπερβάλλουσαν τοῦ ὕδατος πῆξιν μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν: ὃν = crystal, said to be changed (from water) by excess freezing. English says crystal becomes stone, misleading.

edits.old: People say crystal is changed into stone by the extreme freezing of water.
edits.new: People say water is changed into crystal stone by extreme freezing.

fixed: wrong_scripture: fixed — source has στερέωσιν βροντῆς, which is Amos 4:13 (στερεῶν βροντὴν), not Job 37:4.
mistranslation: fixed — source ὃν...μεταποιεῖσθαί φασιν means water is transformed into crystal stone, not crystal into stone.

last_rejected.quote: It is true that all things are in all things
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ μὴν, οὐδὲ εἰ πάντα ἐν ἅπασίν ἐστι
last_rejected.why: The source is concessive and negated: not even if all things are in all things do we accept this. The English turns it into an affirmed premise with 'For that reason', which reverses the logic.
last_rejected.fix: Nor, even if all things are in all things (fire in earth, air in water) and no element is pure, do we accept saying the firmament is one of the simple elements or a mixture of them.
last_rejected.ruling: English keeps 'we do not accept' matching 'Οὐ...καταδεχόμεθα'; 'τούτου ἕνεκεν' preserved; concessive 'οὐδὲ εἰ' to assertive is nuance, conclusion unchanged.

last_rejected.why: The source says the word 'firmament' is applied to a solid nature able to hold back water. 'A different purpose' is not in the source and implies a contrast it does not make.

last_rejected.ruling: No 'different' in 'ἐπί τινος στερρᾶς φύσεως...τετάχθαι'; but 'Καὶ νῦν' signals new use, gloss harmless, solid-nature meaning intact.
